title: Insisting on the rhythm section with Gillespie
summary: He refuses to let Machito's recording sound like American jazz and instructs the bassist.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Bass players: lineage, tone and technique

blocks.x: Even in the last -- the last (inaudible) with Gillespie, they got mad. I know they got mad. He and Dizzy, I say, Dizzy, I don't want this to sound like American (inaudible) playing big jazz. You be now away from the scene too long, and what you are thinking you begin to lose. No. I said, no, no. This Machito band, and it got to sound at least like Machito. (Inaudible) is left to you and to me, Chico (inaudible).

No, no, no, no. I say, all right. Let me handle it. The rhythm, bass and everybody, I'm going to handle that, please. Otherwise we don't record. I don't want to hear a beautiful suite a beautiful (inaudible) buh, buh, buh, buh, (inaudible) and hear that play, tuh-tuh-tuh-tuh-puh-puh-puh-pah. I don't want to hear that.

So I stop putting everything in the (inaudible). I got me guy (inaudible), the best (inaudible) player (inaudible). What you think of that? He say, well, that type of rhythm belong to this (inaudible). I say, that's what it is. I say, let me hear. puh-puh -- I say, do you hear? And now bass player -- now, you know what you got to play? You got to play whoo-dah, kin-kin, koo-koo-kin-kin. That's right. Pah, pah, pah-pah. You (inaudible) is good. I say (inaudible).
All right. You Afro-Cuban, you got to (inaudible).
